newsitem.title: MEXICO: Violence simmers in Mexico ahead of key vote.
newsitem.headline: Violence simmers in Mexico ahead of key vote.

text.p: Oliva Vargas Jimenez was an activist in the leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) for less than a week before gunmen blew her head off with a shotgun.

At dawn on June 4, two gunmen raided the 32-year-mother's wooden shack in this coastal town some 240 miles (400 km) southeast of Mexico City in the state of Oaxaca. They executed her with a shot through the mouth.

To drive home the message, they also murdered her husband Silvano Martinez Salina, 42; her mother Maria Carro Jimenez, 62, and her son Mario Martinez Vargas, 14. Her three other children escaped by hiding under a bed.

Murders and threats against opposition party activists in poor rural states like Oaxaca and neighbouring Guerrero contrast starkly with government claims that key elections next month will be the cleanest, most democratic ever.

On July 6 Mexicans will elect a new lower house of Congress, a quarter of the Senate, six state governors and the mayor of Mexico City. At least eight PRD activists in Oaxaca have been gunned down in the past three months, just as PRD campaigns were gaining steam in the run-up to the vote.

In Guerrero, political violence is also endemic. In late May, the army arrested seven PRD activists and charged them with belonging to a Marxist guerrilla group, the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR). PRD legislators accused state police in February of torture and kidnapping in two villages.

Election violence has also touched the Mexican capital. PRD congress candidate Victor Hugo Campos lost his leg a week ago after being kidnapped, tortured and beaten in a Mexico City taxi assault he blamed on his political militancy.

Oaxaca PRD leader Saul Vicente says the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) is using violence to dissuade people from voting against it. "It is a dirty war so the government can avoid losing the elections," he said after the slaying of the Vargas family.

Police dismiss political motives in the deaths. "Vargas was a PRD member for less than a week so it has nothing to do with politics, we are looking at a revenge murder," Ruben Robles Zarate, chief prosecutor in the case, said.

But residents say Vargas and her family were likely being punished for joining the PRD after the PRI administration gave them land. "It was a totally political assassination," said Antonio Contreras, a bodyguard for Severiano Torres, a cousin of the murdered woman who is also a PRD activist.
Asked for comment, a frightened Torres said, "I cannot talk."
In another Oaxaca town, San Agustin Chayuco, PRD activists say they receive constant death threats.

"I live in fear, they could kill me at any moment," local PRD leader Ciriaco Hernandez said. "Two weeks ago at night they ran through the town, house by house, threatening to kill people who voted for the PRD."

Political violence flared in San Agustin, a town of abobe shacks and banana trees, last August when police shot and killed a PRD supporter at the town's annual festival. PRD activists stormed the town hall and took over the building, forcing PRI Mayor Maximo Flores to flee.

Authorities sent in a 12-man police squad from Oaxaca City, which retook the town hall by force and closed it down. Such is the threat of violence that the town's 1,500 Mixtec Indians have imposed their own nightly curfew.
Hernandez said he and three truckloads of PRD supporters were stopped two weeks ago by the mayor and police as they were returning from a meeting with state farm authorities.
"They confronted us and demanded to know our political intentions. Flores got annoyed and took out his pistol and fired several shots in the air," Hernandez said.
After a tense stand-off, Flores and his men allowed the PRD convoy to continue. The PRD has filed a criminal suit against Flores, who remains in hiding.
Police on guard in the town deny the confrontation ever occurred. "Nothing happened. The news was given out wrongly," said Filogonio Dionisio, the officer in charge of the squad.
